text: The Biological Diversity Act 2002 implements India's commitments under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD). Objectives: conservation, sustainable use, fair and equitable benefit sharing. Three-tier structure: 1) National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) — Chennai, handles foreign entities and IP matters. 2) State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) — each state, handle Indian commercial entities. 3) Biodiversity Management Committees (BMCs) — local bodies at district/block level. For AYUSH: any use of Indian biological resources for commercial/IP purposes requires approval from NBA or SBB.

Section 3 — Foreign nationals, NRIs, and foreign-controlled companies need prior approval from NBA for: 1) Obtaining biological resources from India. 2) Conducting research using biological resources. 3) Bio-survey/bio-utilization. Approval via Form I application. Section 6 — ALL entities (Indian and foreign) need prior approval from NBA before: applying for IP rights in India or abroad based on Indian biological resources. For AYUSH: if you're foreign-controlled or seeking patents, NBA approval is mandatory.

State Biodiversity Boards (SBBs) under Section 23 regulate Indian commercial entities. Section 7: Indian companies, individuals, associations need prior intimation to SBB before obtaining biological resources for commercial utilization. SBB can: prohibit or restrict activities, impose benefit-sharing conditions. Procedure: Apply to SBB of state where resource is obtained. Processing time varies by state. For AYUSH Indian companies: before sourcing medicinal plants commercially, intimate concerned SBB. Multiple states = multiple intimations.

Section 2(c) defines biological resource as: plants, animals, micro-organisms (including parts, genetic material, by-products) with actual or potential use/value. Excludes: human genetic material, listed value-added products where original biological resource is not identifiable. AYUSH context: raw herbs = biological resources (covered). Purified alkaloids/extracts where source herb identifiable = covered. Highly processed chemicals where source unidentifiable = may be excluded. When in doubt, seek NBA guidance.

Section 40 exempts 'normally traded commodities' from some requirements. Notification lists items like: wheat, rice, common vegetables, etc. that are traded as commodities and don't require NBA/SBB approval for general trade. However: if used for research or IP purposes, approval still required. For AYUSH: common spices (turmeric, ginger, black pepper) may be traded commodities, but using them for patent applications still triggers Section 6 NBA approval requirement.

Sections 21 determines benefit-sharing terms for approved access. Benefits can be: 1) Monetary — royalty on sales, upfront payments, milestone payments. 2) Non-monetary — technology transfer, capacity building, research collaboration. NBA/SBB determines terms based on: commercial potential, traditional knowledge involvement, conservation status of resource. Typical royalty: 0.5-5% of sales depending on factors. Benefits flow to: BMCs, communities where resource/knowledge originates, National/State Biodiversity Funds.

Biological Diversity Rules 2004 updated by ABS Regulations 2014 provide detailed procedures: 1) Form I — foreign entity access to bio-resources. 2) Form II — Transfer of research results outside India. 3) Form III — IP applications on Indian bio-resources. 4) Form IV — Third-party transfer of bio-resources. Applications processed within 90-180 days. Fees: Rs 10,000 for Form I, Rs 500 for Form III. Appeal to NBA against SBB decisions.

Section 6/Form III process for patent applications: 1) Apply to NBA before filing patent (in India or abroad). 2) Disclose biological resource used, source, involvement of traditional knowledge. 3) NBA examines and may impose benefit-sharing terms. 4) NBA issues approval letter with conditions. 5) Include NBA approval reference in patent application. Timeline: 3-6 months typically. If patent filed without NBA approval — NBA can oppose the patent, criminal prosecution possible.

Traditional knowledge associated with biological resources gets special protection. Section 36(iv) requires: 1) Prior informed consent from knowledge holders (communities, practitioners). 2) Mutually agreed terms for benefit sharing. People's Biodiversity Registers (PBRs) at BMC level document traditional knowledge. For AYUSH based on traditional Ayurvedic knowledge: get consent from relevant communities, include benefit-sharing provisions, acknowledge knowledge source in applications.

Violations of Biological Diversity Act: Section 55 — Using biological resources without approval: imprisonment up to 5 years, fine up to Rs 10 lakh, or both. Section 55(2) — Repeat offenses: double penalties. Section 56 — Offenses by companies: directors/responsible persons personally liable. Section 59 — NBA can impose penalty (separate from criminal prosecution). For AYUSH: non-compliance is serious — criminal liability, patent opposition, reputational damage. Get proper approvals.

Foreign collaboration triggers NBA requirements: 1) Joint ventures with foreign entities — if using Indian bio-resources. 2) Contract manufacturing for foreign companies. 3) Research collaborations with foreign institutions. 4) Export of bio-resources to foreign partners. 5) Foreign investment/control in Indian company. Assessment: does the arrangement give foreign parties access to Indian biological resources or their benefits? If yes, NBA approval required.

Nagoya Protocol (2010, India party since 2012) is international framework for ABS. Key requirements: 1) Access to genetic resources with prior informed consent of provider country. 2) Benefits shared fairly with provider country. 3) User countries ensure compliance by their users. India implemented through existing BD Act + ABS Regulations. Internationally Recognized Certificate of Compliance (IRCC): NBA approval serves as India's IRCC. For AYUSH exporters: importing countries may require proof of legal sourcing — NBA approval provides this.

AYUSH industry specific considerations: 1) Most AYUSH products use biological resources — BD Act likely applies. 2) Traditional Ayurvedic formulations may involve traditional knowledge — benefit sharing with communities. 3) Cultivated vs wild-collected herbs — both covered if used commercially. 4) NBA has issued guidance for AYUSH industry — consult. 5) Industry associations (ADMA, IDMA) can help navigate requirements. 6) Proactive compliance builds reputation and reduces risk. Treat BD Act compliance as business necessity, not obstacle.

Section 37 allows declaration of 'Biodiversity Heritage Sites' — areas of biodiversity importance. Implications: stricter regulation on access to biological resources from these areas. State government notifies sites with consultation from local bodies. Examples: gene pools of wild relatives of cultivated plants, high endemism areas. For AYUSH: sourcing medicinal plants from heritage sites may require additional permissions. Check if your source region is a notified heritage site.

BMCs at local level (Panchayat/Municipality) under Section 41: 1) Prepare People's Biodiversity Registers documenting local bio-resources and traditional knowledge. 2) Advise on conservation. 3) Levy collection charges for biological resources (Section 41(3)). 4) Manage Local Biodiversity Fund. For AYUSH sourcing at local level: engage with BMCs, pay applicable collection charges, acknowledge local knowledge, consider supporting conservation activities. BMC engagement builds goodwill and ensures legal compliance.
